title: Why You Have to Preach to Yourself First
subtitle: Why a preacher must let the sermon confront him before it confronts the congregation, and how preaching to yourself first guards against hypocrisy and dead delivery.

sections.title: The Easiest Way to Preach Is to Aim It at Them
sections.body:
There is a way to study the Bible that protects you from it entirely.

You read the text looking for them. The greed in this passage belongs to the wealthy in the third row. The pride belongs to the man who challenged you in the meeting. The lukewarm faith belongs to the crowd that comes twice a year. You build the whole sermon as a weapon and you stand safely behind it, firing. And the worst part is that it feels like diligence. You are working hard on the Word. You are just working hard at pointing it everywhere but at your own chest.

This is the oldest temptation in the ministry, and it is nearly invisible from the inside. The monster, as the saying goes, is never the one in the mirror. We see the failure in the room and miss it in the man holding the notes. A sermon prepared this way can be sharp, even true, and still be a kind of hiding. The preacher has handled fire all week and made sure none of it touched him.

sections.title: Let the Text Preach to You First
sections.body:
Before the text is a sermon for them, it is a word to you. Stop there. Stay there.

The right order is brutal and simple. You do not study the passage primarily to preach it. You study it first to be preached to. You sit under it before you stand over it. You ask not what does this say to my people but what does this say to me, the man who is greedy and proud and lukewarm in ways his people will never see. You let it find you. You let it cut. And only when it has done its work in you do you turn to carry it to anyone else.

This is not a technique to make the sermon better, though it will. It is a matter of survival. A preacher who never lets the Word touch him becomes a man who handles holy things with cold hands, who can say true things about God he no longer feels, who knows the doctrine of grace and has not tasted it since seminary. The text was given to you, brother, not just to your assignment. Read it as the patient before you read it as the physician.

sections.title: Stand Inside the Indictment
sections.body:
The most powerful word a preacher can say about sin is we, and he has to mean it.

When you preach against a sin, the people are watching to see where you are standing. If you stand outside it, pointing in, they feel the accusation and brace against it, and the door of the heart closes. But if you stand inside it with them, if you say I did this, I do this, here is where this text caught me this week, something else happens. The defenses drop, because the man with the microphone just confessed first. You did not lower the standard. You located yourself honestly beneath it, and that honesty is a key that turns locks no amount of force will move.

This is not a humble pose to adopt. A performed humility is just pride in a quieter coat, and the people smell it. It is the real thing or it is nothing. The preacher who is genuinely caught by his own text speaks of sin the way a fellow patient speaks of a disease he also carries, not the way a prosecutor reads a charge. We did this. I did this. Now hear what God says to us, because I needed to hear it before any of you did.

sections.title: This Will Cost You Before Sunday
sections.body:
Preaching to yourself first is not a strategy. It is a wound you accept on purpose.

The text that confronts the congregation Sunday morning has to confront you Thursday afternoon, and Thursday afternoon is private and there is no applause for it. You will reach passages that expose the very thing you are still failing at, and the honest move is to let them expose it, to repent before you preach, to take to your own knees what you are about to ask your people to take to theirs. This is slow and it is humbling and it ruins the comfortable distance the office can give you.

It also guards you from the deadliest thing in ministry, which is hypocrisy that you cannot see. The preacher who never sits under his own preaching drifts, by inches, into a man who proclaims a Christ he is no longer walking with, and he is always the last to know. Letting the Word judge you first is the discipline that keeps the seam from closing, the seam between what you say and what you are. Close that seam and you become the German Christian of the pulpit, sincere, fluent, and serving something other than the God whose name you keep on your lips.

sections.title: The People Can Tell the Difference
sections.body:
A sermon that went through the preacher carries something a polished sermon never will.

Congregations are not fooled for long. They can sense the difference between a man delivering content and a man handing over something that cost him. The text that broke you on Thursday lands with a weight on Sunday that no technique can fake, because conviction is contagious and so is its absence. When the people feel that the word in your mouth has already done its work in your life, they trust it. They lean in. They are willing to be cut, because they can see you bleeding too.

This is the whole secret behind preaching that lands and the explanation for preaching that does not. The dead sermon is often technically fine. It is just airless, because the man who gives it was never inside it. The living sermon may be plainer, but the people feel a man who met God in the text and could not keep it to himself.

So before you ask what this passage will do to your people, kneel and let it do its work on you. Preach to yourself first. Preach the rest of your life to yourself first. And let them overhear a man still being saved.
